The whole "feeding people to the SCP" thing seems to be a holdover from the fact that this is a series 1 skip. A lot of old ones mentioned that sort of thing whereas nowadays you need to give a real good reason to justify feeding/sacrificing people to an SCP, otherwise people start to ask why on earth they're doing it.

If the author ever decided to revisit this, I'm sure there could be plenty of improvements, but as it stands, I thought it was interesting as a concept, creepy as hell to imagine, and the line about being able to skip feeding it if someone doesn't take the proper safety precautions got a laugh, so I gave it a +1

item.title: Staff Post
item.content:encoded:
This article is being placed up for review. Check it out, please? We think it could use more attention.

Eeehhh… this one doesn't do anything for me. It's just a big thing that looks like a virus, and kinda imitates how a virus would be if it were made big. The way the effect progresses is confusingly formatted, and the addenda was kind of narmy. Additionally, I don't like how it's intermittently referred to as "SCP-371" or "the virus" or how the first picture is an illustration.

I could see something cool being done with this idea, especially with the second picture, but as it stands there's absolutely nothing here that makes it worth my time. Downvoted.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
It really doesn't seem that much like a virus… just some sort of sea-spider that likes to lay its eggs in other things.

I mean I get that it's injecting the host with its own patterns and whatnot to create more viruses, but… well, so?

This thing is actually kind of less frightening than some actual animals, with just the scare factor that people don't like viruses and find them scary because it's something that can hurt you and do terrible things to you without you seeing it. Once you can see it, it's actually less scary.

This doesn't really evoke any sort of body horror or anything. Even the vague scariness of "Well we don't have a fish or cow handy, may as well feed it a D-class" doesn't even really carry much punch since there's not much reason for them to do so. There's no indication that these are the only specimens alive or that they're even that difficult to come by, so if important research is being done on them (which isn't mentioned even in passing), they could just as easily be allowed to go hungry or die off and then the collection team could go out and get some more. Well, I guess it depends on how these particular researchers view D-class, but since there's no mention of collecting the specimens being particularly difficult or dangerous, that D-class could probably be better used for something else and the collection team could just go swimming again.

"Viruses don't work like that." Try as I might, that was the only thing I ended up thinking throughout this entire thing. You make them out to be some sort of crawling, self-replicating sea monster when they're not even a mass of goo in a super-tiny lipid sheathe. Not even the basest effort to address the contradictions with standard science/reality.

Having some understanding of biology, this screams bad science at me. Downvoted, unfortunately.
